### Give the brief author four rules for each case, and count what a brief shows of them

[`523dd364de34`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/523dd364de34589f6d503b79d85927c006feede3) · [log `87055e7cc0ab`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/87055e7cc0abe270b09bcf7cf705929e21cc61b9dabc202a95b39d31fa590a0f.jsonl.gz)

The user compared six generated briefs (155 cases) with rationale files of their own, which stay private, and wrote the result up as llm-dlc/loops/brief-generation-quality-takeaway.md. The brief author misread and missed nothing, but in every batch it dropped or blurred the second observation that changes one input, three times accepted "either order" where the behaviour defines an order, and reached for a database, JMS or a child process where a public call would show the same. Its own predictions that the merged code is still wrong were a strength worth keeping. The rate did not vary with the size of the list, so the gap is in the instructions. This is now VF-075 in verification/findings.md, with the cause, what landed, the baseline and what the user's next comparison should count.

llm-dlc/loops/brief-generation-template.md gives the author four rules for each case, in the first text in full and in the continue message in short (a later cycle starts after a compaction with the continue message alone): a claim row with the role Variation that repeats the main observation with exactly one input changed and says what each revision should do, the reversal where the behaviour depends on order; the order stated and checked wherever the code under change produces one; the cheapest observation that shows the change, with the reason in the technical notes when more than a public call is needed; and a claim row with the role Remaining defect wherever the landed code still looks wrong. The two are claim rows because the agent that verifies a brief decides every claim row. The author checks the rules before a cycle ends and gives its counts with "The brief is complete" and in its record. The user's handoff is unchanged, and single_run.py renders the template as before.

brief_queue.py counts what a written brief shows of the rules: the cases with a Variation row and those without, the Remaining defect rows, and the cases whose words leave an order open. The brief step of next gives the count when it queues a generated brief (caseRules, a line for the user, the queue's log) and refuses nothing; brief_queue.py rules FILE counts any brief. Over the nine generated briefs on the line (235 cases) it finds no such rows, as the roles did not exist, and 13 cases that leave an order open. The single-agent-run skill page describes the rules and the count for the watcher.

Verified by tests of the texts an author is given, not of the template file: both texts as generate renders them hold each rule (they lacked all four before the change, in both); the text the Codex stand-in was started with and the run's continue message hold them; and so do the first and the continued prompt of an author the queue started, whose brief the brief step then counts. python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed passed 7 of 7 test files, and the lint of the test inventory agrees (two new unit rows). Nothing here runs a prover, so there is no verification job. Not shown yet: that an author follows the rules, which the user's comparison of the next generated list with a rationale file will show.

### Add the register of what is retired, and a check that live files point at it

[`3e2d51c67c98`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/3e2d51c67c988a67a1cd1a45dbcddc167d50d34b) · [log `40c04b2885dc`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/40c04b2885dcf077ec2c3eda0b571f376b26c47697e891999096b559e6198fc3.jsonl.gz)

The user decided on 2026-11-27 that the project converges on one run skill, to be called orchestrate-run, and that every other proof workflow is outdated: multi-agent-brief, the proof loop behind prove-java-change, the loops started by hand, the Sonnet verification loop, and the published plugin with its runtime mode. Nothing is to leave the history of work, and whatever names a retired thing is to say where to find it.

llm-dlc/retired.md is that place: one entry for each thing, with what it was, what replaced it, the names that should no longer turn up in live files, the files that go, and the change that removed it. Every entry is still planned: this change removes nothing. llm-dlc/tools/retired.py reads the entries and lists each paragraph of a live file (instructions, skills, tools and their tests) that names something retired without pointing at the register, and each retired file that is still here. test_retired.py runs it on the repository, so it starts to hold as entries turn retired. With --planned it shows the work ahead: 367 paragraphs in 72 live files and 39 files.

Verified by test_retired.py (5 tests: an entry's form, a failing page and its control once it points at the register, names as whole words, a retired file still present, the generated table of sessions left unread) and by test_costs.py lint. The inventory also gains the rows of nine tests other sessions added without them.

### Move what the run tools share out of the two controllers that are being retired

[`88b0e1015750`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/88b0e1015750d8404581a76d329f1f43fae7a235) · [log `1e20cd4d30a4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/1e20cd4d30a48ec86f513fab3ce51793e4f2aeee97ece5be8b0374703cf9f209.jsonl.gz)

single_run.py and brief_queue.py took landing, trial merges, queue keeping, the nested-run refusal and the clock from brief_run.py (the streams' controller) and watch.py (the proof run's), which are to be retired (llm-dlc/retired.md). Their text is moved, unchanged, into three modules: run_common.py (a run's state, the clock, what a turn cost, jj, the workspaces and loops of a folder, the commits a run made, the refusal to start a run from inside one), landing.py (land, onto_line, trial_merge and the locks they hold) and queue_keeping.py (collect, start_runner, tend). The two old controllers import them, so both still work as before; single_run.py and brief_queue.py no longer import either controller. One wording differs: a merge landed with no message of its own now names the workspace, and the foundation stage passes its own words.

watch.py had also become the home of checks on examples. They move to examples/tools: preflight.py (what each example named lacks before a run takes it; validate_example.py and the numbered handoff call it) and observe.py (the startup-facts and public-observation reports). watch.py's commands of those names call them. preflight.py no longer says which claims a person has reviewed: that record belongs to the proof run, and watch.py adds it for as long as it exists.

Verified by the changed-tests run: 66 of 66 test files passed, among them the two old controllers' own (test_brief_run 54, test_watch 42, test_prove_loop 32), test_single_run (29) and test_brief_queue (12). The moved code has tests of its own that do not go through a retiring controller: test_landing.py (14, on real jj repositories: forward, merge, conflict taken back, another session's files, trace output, a person's decisions, onto_line, a trial merge), test_queue_keeping.py (6), test_run_common.py (9) and test_preflight.py (9). The cost lint agrees.

### Rename the run skill to orchestrate-run, with a page for each kind of run

[`715b7befe26b`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/715b7befe26bd619ddebee5f14e5b86cb1e03cbe) · [log `be9027345ccd`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/be9027345ccd6a31df540bd4265dd83d8a3bb4849634f45821823f82723e6a51.jsonl.gz)

The user decided on 2026-11-27 that the project converges on one run skill and named it orchestrate-run. It is single-agent-run under a new name: its commands (single_run.py, brief_queue.py) and a run's folder (single-NAME) are unchanged, so no record changes.

The one page of 388 lines is now a core page and four beside it. SKILL.md holds what every run needs: the watcher's rules, the request, a run under way, start, watch and report, and a table of the four kinds of run. setup.md, generation.md, queue.md and redaction.md hold the sections of those names, moved as they were, and the core page tells the watcher to read a kind's page in full before acting on it and again after a compaction. The opening no longer describes the watcher by two skills that are being retired; it says this is the repository's one run skill and points at llm-dlc/retired.md for the others.

The by-hand resolution of a landing that conflicts was written only on the proof run's page, which is to be retired: it is now in the operating notes ("A landing that conflicts"), and the skill and landing.py's message point there. The register's entry for single-agent-run is retired, and the check holds for it: no live file names the old skill without pointing at the register.

### Let sync SESSION re-render a session whose transcript is in another workspace's folder

[`77c09789c373`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/77c09789c37318015e4537c47b87d11625387a65) · [log `e41e251cf74b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/e41e251cf74bdd726b9e2526eae17026ce816ea3cb03596612ad6945fe78ab66.jsonl.gz)

On 2026-11-27 the merge of the promotion's record with the line conflicted in the Fable session's manifest: the promotion marked an earlier log uploaded, and the line added a later log. The way to settle such a conflict is to re-render the manifest with sync.py sync SESSION, but transcript_of looked only in this checkout's project folder and its own Codex rollouts, and the Fable transcript is in the queue workspace's folder, so the watcher could not settle it. transcript_of now falls back to the transcript wherever it is on this machine (transcript_anywhere, which VF-074's fix added), never a Codex thread that was only asked a question. A session rendered from another workspace's transcript keeps the workspace its manifest names, whose paths its log has, instead of taking this checkout's; its summary is rendered by that workspace as well. The size total in traces/README.md now counts a log this workspace does not store yet as 0 instead of failing, which a re-render of such a session met. The way to settle the conflict: restore the side whose manifest records the upload (jj restore --from that side the manifest), then sync.py adopt-logs and sync.py sync SESSION, which adds the later log and keeps the URL. Verified: a unit test (a transcript in another workspace's folder is found and is not this checkout's own; with none anywhere the old name is kept); a real sync of the Fable session from a fresh workspace found its transcript, kept its workspace and added its later log after adopt-logs; test_costs run --changed, 23 of 23 files pass; lint agrees.

### ARCHITECTURE.md: the map of who owns what, who may do what and what is not built

[`4006f681db26`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4006f681db26fc4adec717d04c1d4757a8c0a932) · [log `5d2af750c69b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/5d2af750c69bbcea45f7eafa7f89fe38966aabad1a71c6516ac8914937713a44.jsonl.gz)

The user asked for the architecture page to become a first-class file of the project once the run skills had converged, written from their draft and updated to the implementation and the direction as they now are. This is its first version, at the repository's root, for their review.

The page has one path (a person, a watcher, a run, its jobs, a checker, the line, develop, main) with a diagram, the four kinds of run, where the judgment is and where it is not, a table of owners with each one's contract, a table of who may do what and what holds each rule, the record that answers each question, and one section for what is intended and not built: a product entry, the job pipeline the user wants to grow out of /run-verification, fan-out from a manifest, a sealed producer, a worker request, the filter-stop wording, machine-wide run visibility, a run's record and cost (VF-078), the meaning of a trace line (VF-079), network capacity. It also says how a finding becomes the next plan, how something is retired, and how the page is kept. Against the draft: the released product and its mode, the streams' controller and the proof run's watcher are gone from the owners, links are relative so that they resolve at the commit being read, and measurements are left with their owners.

### Give every execution of a job its own attempt folders, and prune by exact attempt

change `wzyqzummrztm` · [log `085632357f1b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/085632357f1b4a287fe236b3482e4a13b2194987ae32dd966e774b2b3f5fcc97.jsonl.gz)

Second slice of the brief for one jobs pipeline, the rest of its gate 'protect and measure': the two evidence-retention risks it names. Until now every run of a job wrote into the same run and work directories, and a rerun cleared them after asking the private archive to keep the earlier attempt; when the archive could not, the bytes went with the folder. And prune asked whether the job's latest captured work directory was verified, which is an earlier attempt's when a later capture failed. The brief queue's cleanup had the same fault with a rule of its own.

Now each execution is an attempt with a durable record and folders of its own (jobs/attempts.py, .state/attempts/ID/NNN-TOKEN/), made before its first output whether or not the archive answers. A rerun clears nothing, and the result names its attempt and the ones before it. pipeline.py recover seals what nothing sealed, where it is: an attempt whose runner died, one whose capture failed, a result set aside, a run directory of the old layout; a runner does it when it starts, and recover --kept-outputs seals VF-080's files. pipeline.py prune removes a work directory only when the job's result is collected, the receipt is of that attempt or a later one, the original sealed from that very attempt is verified in the store, and the folder is still what was sealed; prune --why says why each other stays. brief_queue.py's cleanup calls that prune. A collect that was stopped after it wrote a result, or after that result was committed, is finished by the next one without writing the receipt again. The audit lists unsealed attempts as gaps. artifacts.py takes an attempt number the pipeline gave and answers for exact occurrences.

### Write, run and collect jobs of the second format, and keep a result's questions apart

change `lqkqyulqxulk` · [log `586115e8439b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/586115e8439bc3d06d7865cc9b1c56a55456dd8d2c86d6e0d9e8b371f85aaa55.jsonl.gz)

A job that names a purpose (submit --purpose resolve|build|test|verify|maintenance) is written in the second format, itl-job/v2: a workload, labels, a case, required and optional outputs, a network for its steps, and what a step promises besides its exit code. It runs in the same queue as jobs of the first format, and collect, report, validate and resubmit take it as any other. Every job of the first format runs as it did, and its status means what it meant.

A result of either format now keeps apart what one status word answered at once (jobs/lifecycle.py, one function each, for the runner and for a reader of an old receipt, which marks them derived): execution (what the processes did, and where and why it stopped), fulfillment (fulfilled, unfulfilled with every reason, undetermined), declared (each declared output: added, modified, deleted, unchanged, missing, never-reached, with its producer attempt), timing by scope (queue wait, elapsed, preparation, requested steps, by phase, each measured, derived, partial, not-run or unknown), and the workload's conclusion. A second-format job whose processes all exited as expected and which did not deliver what it declared is failed: a required output that is not there, or a step that promised tests and shows none executed (jobs/evidence.py reads JUnit XML reports or the log's summary lines; VF-070). A regression test expected to fail by assertion is a fulfilled job, and a build that broke before any test is not.

A step declared network none runs in a network namespace with loopback alone, and its record keeps what a probe saw there. A machine that cannot enforce that, or a checkout without the adapter a job names, does not start the job, and status says why. A job that names prerequisites is not started until scheduling by them is built (the next commit). A job records the run its submitter works in (submitted.run), read from the loop's systemd scope (VF-077).

Verified: jobs/test_formats.py (11 tests, each in a throwaway repository through jobs/pipeline.py) shows the three jobs the brief's second gate names: a non-Java artifact job on a PATH with no checker, submitted, run beside a first-format job, collected, reported, validated and resubmitted; real unit tests counted from the log, and a step that compiled only failing its promise with exit 0; a stand-in for JBMC's refutation giving status passed, fulfillment fulfilled, conclusion refuted, in both formats. jobs/test_lifecycle.py (6) reads the brief's timing fixture from its committed receipt: 41.0 s elapsed measured, 41.0 s preparation derived, requested steps not-run. jobs/test_evidence.py (5). The tests of what changed: 37 of 37 Python test files passed (verification/test_pipeline.py 52 tests, test_capture.py, the keepers' tests among them); the cost lint and the retirement check are clean.

### Give every job one state with its reason, in one view the keepers read as data

change `vywknlrlrttr` · [log `0c5f71ee9a19`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/0c5f71ee9a19ae0482f4bd523298f5afa68c6450578c97f0a72d7f608085064a.jsonl.gz)

A committed job that has not started is now in exactly one state, decided in one place (jobs/scheduling.py) for the runner and for every report: invalid (its file is not a job; the reason carries the path and the revision), unschedulable (this machine cannot run it as written), blocked (a prerequisite ended without passing, or nobody submitted it), waiting (a prerequisite has not finished), deferred (a runner at work holds it back: no room, a priority it leaves) or queued. The runner schedules by prerequisites: a job with needs starts once that job, or one that supersedes it, has passed; one whose prerequisite failed is blocked with nothing run and no attempt consumed, and resubmitting the prerequisite releases it with its own file unchanged. A runner whose remaining jobs all wait for something it is not running says so and ends.

python3 jobs/pipeline.py view prints the one view of every job (itl-job-lifecycle/v1): the snapshot's revision and what could and could not be read, every job's state and reason, its prerequisites, claim, attempts and result (its questions apart, derived for a receipt that did not keep them), totals with their unit and denominator, and the last collect's hooks. status is that view as lines, and status --json keeps its shape of before. wait --json and collect --json say as data what their lines say; a hook that failed after a collect is kept and named until a later collect runs it.

A queue that could not be read is unknown and never empty: view exits 4 with idle null, status begins with what was NOT READ, and the keepers return unknown instead of zero jobs (run_common.jobs returned an empty queue for any answer it could not parse). The keepers (queue_keeping.py, run_common.py, single_run.py, sync.py's nudge, the brief queue's prune) call jobs/pipeline.py and read the view and collect --json: the regular expressions over the pipeline's lines and the test for '; cannot run here:' are gone. The /run-verification skill names the same entry point and the states. The runner's word for a job it will never start is unschedulable, where it said deferred.

Verified: jobs/test_scheduling.py (8 unit tests of the decision), jobs/test_formats.py Prerequisites (3, in throwaway repositories: a dependent after its prerequisite, a blocked one with no attempt folder that runs after the prerequisite is resubmitted, a runner that ends with a job left waiting), jobs/test_view.py (5: every state from uncommitted to collected with totals that add up, a corrupt spec with path and revision, deferred as a job's own step read it during a run with one worker, a derived receipt, a repository git cannot read giving exit 4 and idle null, the typed wait and collect with a hook that exits 3). The tests of what changed: 41 Python test files, 40 passed and llm-dlc/tools/test_single_run.py failed one assertion on the summary's old wording, which is updated with a case for the unknown queue and passes.

### Let a running case ask for more setup: one request, a resolution job, a receipt that wakes it

change `ytnxopmtrrvz` · [log `5fbdbeba28eb`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/5fbdbeba28ebcd433bfaf669ab12be3f19374afe66d036f7fc63d29c31f564b4.jsonl.gz)

A job can now need a readiness operation (submit --needs-readiness OPERATION.json; jobs/readiness.py): what 'ready' means for one task (the revision, module, task, toolchain and platform it describes, the level asked for, the prepared base it starts from, the task's own steps, the outputs they must leave, the repositories and the pinned inputs with their digests). The operation's key is the digest of all of that but the title, who asks and the estimate, so two cases that need the same thing share one request and one resolution. The job that asks waits, alone; the view lists the request, unanswered until a receipt is ready or withheld or a job is on its way. The watcher admits a resolution job by committing what 'pipeline.py resolve' writes (queue_keeping.admit, at each look), and it runs through the same scheduler, on a runner whose settings name the sources it may fetch from (fetch_allow; with none a job that fetches is unschedulable) and within its fetch slots (fetch_slots, 10). Only a resolution job's steps are told those sources.

The resolution is rounds: lay the base and what is staged so far into a view, run the task with no network and the base bound read-only, read its log for the module it could not find, fetch exactly that (verified by the repository's checksum, or by the operation's digest for a pinned input), and go again; a second stage that asks for a prerequisite nobody knew of is one more round. It ends ready when the task ran through offline and left its outputs, and only then publishes the staged files as a read-only bundle by one rename, with a receipt: every round, what was fetched from where, the probe of the offline run, the bundle's digest. Otherwise readiness is withheld with the stage and a named outcome (absent, repository-unavailable, digest-mismatch, unauthorized-source, undiagnosed, no-progress, round-limit, output-mismatch) and nothing is published. A ready receipt wakes the job that asked: the runner reads the bundle in full against the receipt (one that changed since blocks the job until it is resolved again), lays it over the base as a view of that attempt's own, and binds the base and the bundle read-only for a step with no network. A withheld readiness blocks its consumer by the outcome's name; 'resolve KEY --again' resolves the same request once the cause is put right.

Verified on a made-up nested build served from 127.0.0.1 (its first stage needs a tool distribution and a BOM, its second asks for a module nobody named; it refuses to pass if it can reach the repository or write into the prepared inputs). jobs/test_readiness.py (11): ready after three rounds with four verified files; an identical request reuses the receipt and another toolchain or task is another key; a changed bundle is refused and resolved again; absent, digest-mismatch, repository-unavailable, unauthorized-source, undiagnosed, no-progress and output-mismatch each withhold with nothing published. jobs/test_delayed_setup.py (3, with a runner at work): the unrelated job finishes while both consumers wait and nothing has been fetched; one resolution job is admitted for the one request; both consumers start after it, run once, offline, on the bundle its conclusion names, and the repository was asked once for each file; a withheld BOM blocks its consumer by name until it is resolved again; a runner that may fetch from nowhere does not start the resolution. llm-dlc/tools/test_queue_keeping.py: the watcher admits once by a commit, then starts the runner. The tests of what changed: 44 of 44 Python test files passed. S48 itself, on the real cache, is the next commit's job.

### Ask for S48's setup as one request from a cache made insufficient, with three controls (verification pending)

change `tnwmnzynpotl` · [log `36cbbb71f591`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/36cbbb71f59139efb70dc19c7c229d0c1225c3b6088f854fadc5683882dacf3f.jsonl.gz)

The brief's gate 3 names S48 (Spring Boot example 635, PR #51551) as the case that qualifies delayed setup: on 2026-11-27 its two Maven WAR builds were made readable only after a chain of failed jobs, each naming one more missing input. This commit prepares the replay of that case through the new readiness path and queues it as job 20261128-000950-replay-s48-s-delayed-setup-as-one-reques, which has not run yet.

What the job runs. verification/merged-pr-links/s01-s50/maven-war/readiness_gate.py builds a throwaway repository holding this line's pipeline, lays the S cache with what the original chain lacked taken out (the ActiveMQ BOM 6.1.8 in both the Maven and the Gradle layout, and the Maven 3.9.13 distribution), and submits one consumer job that needs the operation in readiness-operation.json beside it. It then checks that there was one logical request and one resolution job, that no consumer job failed on the way, that the four WARs were read offline on both pins and equal the committed parent.json and fix.json, that an unrelated job finished during the wait, and three controls that must each refuse with their own reason: a withheld BOM (absent), a wrong digest for the Maven distribution (digest-mismatch) and a repository that does not answer (repository-unavailable). It writes readiness-gate.json with every check and a timeline, and exits 0 only when every check passed. The watcher's runner is still the pipeline of the default checkout, so the job itself is of the first format and runs the new scheduler inside its one step.

What changed in the mechanism for it. A view of a cache can now walk named folders file by file (view.walk) instead of linking them whole, so one module can be withheld from a tree of thousands, and a withheld path ending in / leaves an empty folder. What a build tool says it lacks is read as coordinates from Gradle's and Maven's own lines (missing_coordinates), including the line the original failure printed. The resolver lays .sha1 files beside what it fetched.

### Leave Gradle's record of the withheld BOM out of S48's base, and run the gate again (verification pending)

change `pxoswmwztksp` · [log `513ded32f542`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/513ded32f5425f2bb5aa387257be146204f910580d5414ec526644877ab83fef.jsonl.gz)

The S48 gate's first run (job 20261128-000950-replay-s48-s-delayed-setup-as-one-reques) passed 10 of 13 checks and failed where it matters: the resolution job stopped in its second round at no-progress and published nothing, so the consumer never ran. This commit corrects the cause, which was in the gate's own base, and queues the second run as job 20261128-003144-replay-s48-s-delayed-setup-as-one-reques, which supersedes the first and has not run yet.

What happened. Round 1 fetched the pinned Maven distribution and ran the task offline until createResolvedBom lacked org.apache.activemq:activemq-bom:6.1.8. Round 2 fetched the BOM's POM from Maven Central, laid it in Maven's layout, and the task went past that stage and a hundred compile tasks before another task asked for the same POM. The base had left out the BOM's file in Gradle's store and kept Gradle's descriptor of the module. Maven Central comes before the replay's file mirror in each subproject's repositories, and Gradle takes the first repository with a record of a module, so it asked Central, offline, for a file that was gone and never read the mirror. readiness-operation.json now leaves the descriptor out too, and says in base.why what its state is: stricter than the one VF-076's rounds began in, where the files' dates show the BOM present since the setup phase and only the Maven distribution absent.

What changed in the mechanism. The no-progress reason quotes the line that asked again and says where the files were laid, since the usual cause is a second tool reading another place. A receipt repeats the operation's base.why beside its list of what was left out, and claims nothing itself about whether that state ever existed. The gate's check and the pages no longer call the base a reconstruction of an earlier state.

The results page has the first run's thirteen checks one by one, the correction, the limit it showed (the resolver lays a module in Maven's layout only, so a build that can read a module from nowhere but Gradle's own cache is beyond it), and the table of where each gate stands brought up to date.

Verified: the tests of what changed, 9 of 9 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed), jobs/test_readiness.py with the new wording among them; the gate's logic again passes 16 of 16 checks on the made-up nested build; the corrected view is laid in 0.14 s with the BOM absent in all three places. ### Name the runner of another workspace in the view, and the jobs it has claimed

change `olvzzxqsotxy` · [log `e3a36ba00fd9`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/e3a36ba00fd9f2f024cea7aab4e5c6ad1a685d2f5891b9ea83bd42f93ec1b130.jsonl.gz)

A repository has one runner at a time, whichever workspace it was started in, and an agent that submits from a workspace of its own is never where it is: the watcher's runner, in the default workspace, runs its jobs. Until now such an agent's view said queued, no runner at work, for the whole time its job ran. That is the commonest reader of the view, given an account that was wrong; this run's second S48 job showed it.

The view now reads the lock all workspaces of a repository share (it never takes it) and, in the workspace that lock names, the claims of its runner. runner.elsewhere gives that runner's pid, its workspace and the jobs it has claimed. A job it has claimed is running here too, with the workspace in its reason and in its claim; one it has not yet claimed is queued, and the reason names the runner that will find it; a job that needs one running there waits. status prints the same, wait --json carries runner.elsewhere and still answers no-runner at once (there is nothing here to wait for), and nudge says that a runner elsewhere finds the change at its next look at the queue, since it only reaches this workspace's runner. Nothing is written in the other workspace.

A lock nobody holds any more, or one that names this workspace, names no runner elsewhere. The other workspace's state is looked for where a workspace keeps it by default; when it is not there, the runner is named and what it runs is said to be not seen.

Also in this commit: a control from the brief for readiness levels (a receipt at one level answers no request at another: the S batch's 98 task graphs all configured and 41 of its 49 builds then failed for setup reasons), and three decisions recorded in the results page (30 to 32).

Verified: jobs/test_view.py (7 tests, two new, with a stand-in process as the runner of another workspace), and the tests of what changed, 37 of 37 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed). On the real queue the view of this workspace showed the gate's job running in the runner of the default workspace while it ran.

### Let an offline Gradle build read what a resolution fetched, through a file repository in the view (verification pending)

change `qpylqxowxmtu` · [log `6c673ab9b230`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/6c673ab9b230f1a142404a03a95876cbf27597f0a8f4307cfd254d1482f0751c.jsonl.gz)

S48's gate passed with a replay that brings its own file mirror of the retained caches. An ordinary Gradle build has none: offline, it reads a remote repository's modules from Gradle's own cache and nowhere else, and only Gradle writes that cache with its records. A module the resolver lays in Maven's layout was therefore invisible to it, and a resolution for such a build would have stopped at no-progress, as S48's first run did. That is the commonest offline miss of a domain run, and it was the limit the results page recorded.

Two changes close it for the usual case. Every readiness view now carries a Gradle init script and names it to the steps (ITL_READINESS_GRADLE_INIT, with ITL_READINESS_M2 for the view's Maven-layout folder): a build run with -I gets a file repository over that folder, ahead of its own repositories, for its projects, its build scripts' class paths and its plugins. A file repository is read whatever --offline says. A build that keeps its repositories in its settings gets it there, and one that declares no plugin repository keeps Gradle's default beside it. And a module whose POM says it was published with Gradle's module metadata is fetched with its .module file, which Gradle requires beside such a POM. A consumer job's result records what its steps were told (readiness[].tools).

The gate for it is queued as job 20261128-011602-a-gradle-build-reads-offline-a-library-t and has not run. verification/merged-pr-links/s01-s50/gradle-module/gate.py uses the class of S48's gate on Spring Boot's core module at S48's parent pin: the S cache is laid without org.jspecify:jspecify in Gradle's file store, Gradle's descriptors and Maven's local repository (a made state, said in the operation); one resolution job has to read the library's name from Gradle's own words, fetch its POM, .module and JAR, and prove the compile offline; the consumer then compiles the module itself with no network, and its compiled.json must be byte for byte the resolution's. compile.sh fails if either Gradle cache holds the library after the build, so the file repository is the only place it can have been read from. For that, S48's gate script gained a readback held to the resolution's own output where there is no committed copy, and its record-writing end became a function both gates use.

Verified without Gradle: jobs/test_readiness.py (the made-up module is fetched with its .module file, and the build's step is given both variables), the tests of what changed, 43 of 43 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed), the S48 gate's logic again 16 of 16 on the made-up nested build after the refactor, and the Gradle gate's view laid in 0.13 s with the library absent in all three places. What the init script does in a real Gradle build is verified only when the job's result is read; its handling of repositories kept in settings and of plugins is written and not run. The script inventory is regenerated (98 scripts, the new ones supported).

### Give Gradle a file repository over the fetched modules alone, and run its gate again (verification pending)

change `rxmsnylqpuxz` · [log `09daf6538f03`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/09daf6538f03abe7a03b28b73ea54d077cf7181dac7447eced7c6c469dcd7ea9.jsonl.gz)

The first run of the gate for the readiness view's Gradle init script (job 20261128-011602-a-gradle-build-reads-offline-a-library-t) failed, and showed two things. The script works in a real build: after round 1 stopped on org.jspecify:jspecify:1.0.1, missing for buildSrc's class path, the resolver fetched its POM, its Gradle module metadata and its JAR, and in round 2 Gradle read the library from the file repository. And the repository was over too much: the view's whole Maven-layout folder, which is mostly the base's Maven local repository, where plexus-utils 3.6.0 is a POM with no JAR. Being first in the build's list, the file repository answered for that module, and Gradle then looked for the JAR there and nowhere else, though its own cache had the module whole. The resolution ended undiagnosed, because Gradle's wording for one missing file of a known module was not one the resolver read.

Both are corrected here. A view now lays the fetched modules apart, in Maven's layout, each whole by the way it is fetched (ITL_READINESS_FETCHED_M2), and the init script's file repository is over those alone; ITL_READINESS_M2 stays the whole folder, for a Maven build. And the resolver reads 'Could not find a-v.jar (g:a:v)', so a module that is a bare POM in a repository Gradle does consult is fetched whole in the next round.

The gate is queued again as job 20261128-012905-a-gradle-build-reads-offline-a-library-t, which supersedes the first and has not run. The results page records the first run and what was corrected.

Verified without Gradle: jobs/test_readiness.py (the fetched modules are laid apart with nothing of the base's own, and Gradle's wording is read as its coordinate), jobs/test_delayed_setup.py, the gate's logic 16 of 16 on the made-up nested build, and the tests of what changed, 43 of 43 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed). change `typnwnxwvrnt` · [log `901c3b86ab54`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/43b290ac-3fdc-4f32-8f05-45e7bcb78ce2/901c3b86ab54ebd178adb24a82c65e3b15f593c7213688259c8f6c07ec435b8b.jsonl.gz)

Two things, from a review of this line against its brief by three reviewers that read the code afresh (their findings are being worked through; the results page will list each).

The offline proof was weaker than the page said. A readiness task, and the steps of the job that then runs on the bundle, had no network and a read-only base, but the runner's whole home directory was there to read and write: a Maven build that set no local repository would have passed on ~/.m2. Now such a run has an empty home directory and an empty /tmp of its own (jobs/sandbox.py, alone), its work to write in, and the view, the base, the bundle and the paths the operation declares under reads (a JDK) bound read-only; the variables that point a build tool at a cache of its own are not handed down, and a job that needs a readiness has no network in any step. The two gates' operations declare the JDKs they read, so their keys changed and both are run again: jobs 20261128-021235-replay-s48-s-delayed-setup-as-one-reques and 20261128-021235-a-gradle-build-reads-offline-a-library-t.

The control the brief names beside S48 had only been shown on made-up fixtures: the S batch's first setup jobs, 41 of 49 failed for setup reasons though all 98 dry runs had configured. verification/merged-pr-links/s01-s50/setup-control/ replays them: the S cache laid as it was after the setup's first resolution pass, each case a job of one manifest that needs its builds and landed tests ready at both pins, and a folder made from the retained cache as the one authorised source (nothing is asked of a repository). Job 20261128-021235-replay-five-of-the-s-batch-s-first-setup runs five cases, four at a time.

What the resolver gained for real dependency graphs, each with a test in jobs/test_readiness.py (21 tests): base.asOf leaves out what a cache wrote after a time; task.independent runs every step of a round, so one round learns what both pins lack; a module comes with the parent POMs its POM names; a file a tool names beside a module's JAR is fetched by its name, and Maven's four- and five-part coordinates and a Gradle plugin asked for by its id are read; the level tests-run is shown by evidence of executed tests, not said; a file fetched and verified once is kept by its address and not asked for again by another operation.

And what the review found wrong in that same code, fixed here: a parent POM whose checksum could not be fetched stayed in staging and was published unverified; an absent .sha1 passed for an absent file; a source was allowed by string prefix, and a redirect was followed anywhere; two resolutions of one key could overwrite each other; the scheduler read a whole bundle at every pass; a job's own environment was dropped by the clean one; the batch's lock file sat where jj would commit it; the archive capture raised on an output declared as an object.

Verified: the 44 test files the change selects ran before the review fixes, 43 passed and the script inventory needed regenerating (done); after the fixes the readiness, delayed-setup, batch, fan-out, formats, sandbox and inventory tests pass. The three jobs are the verification on real builds.

The three jobs of the commit before ended in seconds, and for the right reason: with an empty home, the tasks could not read ~/.cache/in-the-loop/git-mirrors/spring-boot.git, where the base's worktrees keep their objects. ## 1. The role names `Variation` and `Remaining defect`

- **What the takeaway said:** add a second observation per case, and keep predictions of remaining defects as a separate prediction with its own observation. It did not say what form they take in the brief.
- **What I added:** each is a claim row of its own with a fixed role, beside the handoff's `Intent`, `Control` and `Challenge` rows.
- **Why:** the verifying agent decides every claim row, so a row gets checked where a sentence of prose may not. A fixed role name also makes the rows countable.
- **Cost:** a case has four or more claim rows where it had three, so the domain run has more to decide per case.
- **Overlap you should judge:** your handoff already defines `Challenge` as "one variation or second public boundary". I told the author to write `Variation` beside it, not in place of it, so an author may write two near-identical rows. The alternative is to drop the new role and have the template require that the `Challenge` row be the single-variable repeat. That gives fewer rows, but loses the "second public boundary" use of `Challenge`.

It is a working architecture for adopting the repository, pinned to `develop` at `8970c059` (2026-11-27). It treats the changes in the implementation brief as proposals until their code and acceptance evidence land.

## The central path

- **Two workflows share the word "watcher".** In repository development a watcher takes a brief through optional generation, setup and one domain-agent run. In the released product a user brings a Java change to `/prove-java-change`. The document asks you to name the workflow, actor and entry point when handing work over.
- **The domain agent owns the expensive judgment.** That is deciding what behaviour a change should preserve or alter, choosing a falsifiable public history, and supplying a receiver and inputs.
- **Everything mechanical should be deterministic tools or verification jobs.** That covers pinning revisions, preparing deployments, binding methods, generating callers, replaying and evaluating evidence.
- **A new model session is a cost.** It consumes delegated resources and needs its own run record.

## Who owns what

| Concern | Owner |
|---|---|
| Agent entry and mode | `CLAUDE.md`, `mode.py`, the plugin and skill aliases |
